title: Ryan McLeod's Quiet Start Hides Fine Chances and Bad Luck
dek: Two points in eight games look thin, but his chances, his skating and his line's results say the story is mostly about finishing and luck.
text:
## Who he is

Ryan McLeod is a 27-year-old left-shot forward, 6'3" and 198 pounds, born in Mississauga, Ontario, with a hometown listed as TOR. He wears number 71 for the Buffalo Sabres. Edmonton drafted him in the second round of the 2018 draft, 40th overall, and he spent 219 games with the Oilers before moving to Buffalo, where he has now played 168 games.

Before this season his career line was 379 games, 66 goals, 116 assists and 182 points. With this season included he sits at 387 games, 67 goals, 117 assists and 184 points. That is a middle-six forward's résumé, a player whose value has tended to come from how he plays more than from the scoresheet. Last season in Buffalo he played all 81 games and scored 14 goals and 40 assists for 54 points, with an expected goals rate of 0.50 per 60 minutes.

## What the season looks like so far

The surface numbers are modest. In eight games he has one goal and one assist, two points, none of them on the power play. He has seven shots on goal, three hits and two blocks, and he averages 15.55 minutes a night.

Among forwards across the league, those numbers put him well down the lists: 244th in points, 262nd in his own expected goals and 184th in ice time, each out of 388. The ice-time rank is the useful one. He is a regular but not a featured forward, and a player in that spot has a limited number of chances to produce.

Eight games is a small sample, and a single bounce in either direction changes how that looks. Everything below should be read with that in mind.

## Chances versus results

The gap between what he has produced and what the model expected is small, which is the first thing worth noting. His own expected goals are 1.08, and he has one actual goal, a difference of minus 0.08. In other words, his own shooting has done about what his shot quality predicted. If he is underperforming, it is not because he is missing good looks.

The bigger gap is around him. With McLeod on the ice, Buffalo has scored 8.23 fewer goals than the chances deserved. That is a large number for a few weeks of games, and it reaches him mostly through assists. It matters because a player gets credit for points when his teammates finish, and the model says the teammates have not been finishing. The flag on his page, "Due," points at exactly this: results that have lagged well behind the underlying play, a gap that tends to close.

The underlying play itself is decent. At five-on-five, Buffalo has had 53.17 percent of the expected goals with him on the ice, so his shifts have tilted the quality of chances in his team's favor. The team as a whole sits at 52.1 percent. The team-impact measure is almost flat, a team share of expected goals 0.25 percentage points worse with him, so he is not driving the team's play up or down. He is a neutral piece on a team that is controlling chances modestly well.

## Role and ice time

The workload has dipped. He has averaged 15.55 minutes over these eight games, and the data says that is 2.06 minutes a game below his usual. Two minutes a night is meaningful for a forward at his level, roughly the difference between a regular middle-six shift count and a reduced one.

The game log shows how uneven it has been. He played 18.6 minutes in the 5-4 win at Toronto on October 15, his high for the stretch, and just 12.0 minutes in the 4-3 win over Chicago on October 3, his low. In between he ranged from 14.2 to 16.9. There is no clean trend there, only a lineup that has shuffled him around.

His production in the log is thin. The one goal came October 12 against Florida, a 5-3 home win in which he took two shots and generated 0.26 expected goals. The one assist came October 1 in the 6-3 loss at Columbus. He went pointless in the other six games.

## Where his shots come from

The location data is encouraging, even if it is a tiny sample. Of his nine unblocked shots, four came from inside 15 feet, and those four carried 0.7 expected goals and produced his one goal. Another two came from 15 to 30 feet (0.2 expected goals), and three came from beyond 30 feet (0.1 expected goals). His average shot distance is 25.7 feet.

The pattern says the quality is concentrated close to the net, and the distance mix is somewhat bottom-heavy: those three long shots contributed almost nothing. Looking at where his shots on goal landed, the areas are spread out: one each from the low slot, the crease, the high slot, the right circle and the center point. The crease shot is the goal. Nothing there looks like a single repeatable habit, which is what you would expect from a player with seven shots on goal.

## How he skates and shoots

The tracking data gives his skating a clear edge over his shot. His top speed is 23.41 mph, which sits at the 99th percentile, essentially among the fastest skaters tracked. He has also logged 31 bursts over 20 mph. That speed is the foundation of what he does well, and it is a big part of why a player with modest scoring numbers can still hold a steady role: he can pressure defenders, create separation and cover ground.

His shot is a different story. His hardest shot is 73.1 mph, which is only the 18th percentile. This is a player who does not rely on velocity, and that makes the close-range shot map more sensible. With a below-average release, the chances that count for him are the ones near the crease, where speed matters less than position.

## How the model sees him

The model projects his own scoring at 0.59 expected goals per 60 minutes, a bit above last season's 0.50. It estimates that with him on the ice, Buffalo should generate 3.1 expected goals for per 60 minutes. It also puts the share of on-ice goals he gets a point on at 0.6.

The model blends this season with last season and his role, because a few weeks of games is too few to trust alone. That is the right instinct here. Eight games of results, good or bad, say little by themselves.

Over his last eight games, which are the same eight, the model expected 4 points from him and he has 2. It expected 1.3 goals and he has 1. His own expected goals of 1.1 sit just under the 1.2 that would be usual for his ice time, and Buffalo's expected goals for with him on the ice, 5.8, trail his usual 6.4. So there is a mild dip in the process, not just in the results, but nothing dramatic.

## What to watch next

Three things matter most. First is ice time. If his minutes drift back toward his usual level, his chances should follow, and the production gap has more room to close. If they keep sliding below 15, the role may be shrinking, and that changes the outlook more than any scoring stretch would.

Second is whether Buffalo's finishing recovers with him on the ice. That 8.23-goal shortfall is the biggest driver of his thin line, and finishing on that scale rarely stays that low for long. If the team's shooting normalizes, assists should come with it.

Third is shot quality. His inside-15-foot shots are doing the work, so watch whether he keeps getting there. A shift toward more long attempts would be a worse sign than a goalless week.

What would change the picture: if his own expected goals start sliding below last season's 0.50 per 60, the problem would be real rather than lucky. If the team's chance share with him on the ice slips below its overall mark, he would be a drag instead of a neutral piece. Neither has happened yet. For now this looks like a fast, close-range forward whose line has simply missed on its chances.
